strengths: The paper is well motivated with a clear empirical characterization of the problem: Figures 2-6 and Tables 1-2 convincingly show that FCFS scheduling causes severe head-of-line blocking and that static batch token limits are suboptimal across hardware/load conditions, directly justifying the proposed design.

Proposition 1 provides a clean theoretical argument for why relying on total output length alone (as in prior SJF-style schedulers) is insufficient in augmented LLM serving, motivating the need to explicitly model API return length and context-handling policy in the scheduling value.

The two-stage scheduling design (prediction-based Stage I, runtime-corrected Stage II, plus an anti-starvation term) is a sensible engineering approach to the noted problem of prediction-error amplification in single-stage predictive schedulers.

Evaluation is fairly extensive: multiple GPUs (4090, H800, 2xA100), two models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B), two datasets (Merge, ToolBench), multiple workload types (Poisson, fixed-count, Gamma/bursty), and multiple metrics (goodput, TTFT, normalized latency, P95 tail latency, TPOT, SLO attainment), with a component-wise ablation (Figure 10) and time breakdown (Table 4) showing negligible prediction overhead.

The dynamic token-batching mechanism is simple, well motivated by the batch-token-limit sensitivity study in Table 1, and is shown via ablation to contribute a real, though smaller, portion of the overall improvement.
weaknesses: The comparison baselines (vLLM, InferCept) both use plain FCFS scheduling; the related-work section explicitly cites several existing output-length or embedding-based predictive schedulers for LLM serving but the paper never empirically compares against any of them, only qualitatively dismissing them as unsuitable for augmented LLM inference. This leaves open whether a substantial fraction of AugServe's reported 4.7-33.1x gain over vLLM/InferCept is attributable to the novel API-aware scheduling versus simply adding any predictive or SJF-style reordering on top of FCFS.

The very large reported speedups (up to 33x throughput, 96% TTFT reduction) appear highly sensitive to the chosen SLO (TTFT below 1s), which the paper's own analysis suggests is extremely strict relative to typical external API latencies; under such a tight threshold nearly all FCFS-queued requests will trivially fail regardless of scheduling sophistication, which may inflate the apparent advantage rather than isolating the contribution of the proposed scheduler. No sensitivity analysis over a range of SLO thresholds is shown in the main text, only a single 5xSLO variant in the appendix that still shows similarly extreme gains without deeper analysis of the cause.

The output-length predictor achieves only 65 percent bucket accuracy on the Merge dataset and an API-duration MSE of about 5 seconds, yet the paper offers no sensitivity analysis of end-to-end performance to prediction quality to substantiate the claim that this accuracy is sufficient and that Stage II correction fully compensates for these errors.

No mention of code or artifact release, exact hyperparameter settings used in experiments, or repeated runs with variance or confidence intervals; results appear to be single-run point estimates, which limits reproducibility.

The many cost formulas rely on several simplifying assumptions such as uniform per-token memory footprint, deterministic forward time, and linear swap-cost models that are not empirically validated against measured system costs, leaving unclear how robust the scheduling value estimates are when these idealized cost models are violated in real deployments with variable batch compositions.

The core techniques largely combine existing ideas, namely context-handling policy selection following InferCept, output-length-bucket prediction following prior scheduling work, and iteration-level batching following Orca, so the novelty mainly lies in the specific two-stage value formulation for the augmented-LLM setting, which is a reasonable but somewhat incremental contribution.

strengths: The motivational study (Section 3) is empirically grounded, using real profiling (queueing CDFs, goodput vs. request rate, batch-token sweeps) to clearly illustrate the HoL blocking problem under FCFS and the sub-optimality of static batch token limits in augmented LLM serving.

Proposition 1 gives a clean, intuitive justification for why scheduling purely by total request length is insufficient when API return lengths vary, motivating the need for return-length-aware scheduling.

The evaluation spans multiple models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B), multiple hardware platforms (4090, H800, 2xA100), two datasets (Merge, ToolBench), and multiple workload generators (Poisson, fixed-count, Gamma/bursty), which is a reasonably broad experimental matrix.
The ablation study (Figure 10, Table 4) attempts to isolate the contribution of dynamic batching vs. two-stage scheduling and shows the prediction module's runtime overhead is negligible (<1%).
The problem being addressed (SLO-aware serving for tool-augmented LLM inference) is practically relevant given the growing use of function calling/MCP in production LLM services.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an incremental combination of existing ideas: SJF/output-length-prediction-based scheduling (already explored in S3, FastServe, Fu et al.'s learning-to-rank scheduler, Zheng et al.) merged with InferCept's context-handling cost model, plus a fairly standard memory-utilization-driven dynamic batch size controller. The paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally novel beyond stitching these components together.

Only two baselines are compared (vLLM and InferCept), both of which use plain FCFS scheduling and (apparently) static batch token limits. No comparison is made against other predictive-scheduling LLM serving systems (e.g., S3, FastServe, learning-to-rank scheduling) that are cited as related work, making it hard to isolate whether gains come from the proposed two-stage design or simply from any reasonable move away from FCFS/static batching.

It is unclear whether the batch token limits for vLLM/InferCept baselines were tuned to their respective optimal operating points before comparison; given Table 1 shows huge throughput variation (0.10 to 0.41 req/s) purely from this hyperparameter, an unfair or default configuration for baselines could substantially inflate the reported 4.7-33.1x and 3.3-13.2x improvements, which otherwise appear implausibly large for a scheduling-level optimization.

The scheduling-value formulas (Eqs. 4-26) are heuristic engineering cost estimates (not derived from or validated against a principled throughput/latency optimization objective), and no sensitivity analysis is provided for the many introduced hyperparameters (α, β_low, β_high, γ, bucket discretization for output length prediction) that likely strongly affect performance.

Prediction accuracy is modest (65% bucket accuracy on Merge, API duration MSE ~5s), yet the paper does not analyze how this uncertainty propagates into scheduling-value errors or final throughput/latency; the claim that Stage II 'corrects' errors is asserted rather than quantitatively demonstrated via a controlled study (e.g., prediction accuracy ablation).

No error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-run variance are reported anywhere in the throughput/latency figures or tables, despite the stochastic nature of Poisson/Gamma arrival processes and the relatively small 2k-request or 30-minute experiment windows; some reported numbers show large, possibly noise-driven jumps (e.g., vLLM SLO attainment 98.4% at 4.0 req/s dropping to 22.7% at 5.0 req/s), raising concerns about result reliability.
No code, artifact, or implementation details (e.g., exact prediction model training setup beyond brief mention, hyperparameter values used in experiments) are provided, limiting reproducibility.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations or discussion section addressing generalization beyond the tested models/datasets, scalability to larger models/clusters, or robustness to adversarial/edge-case workloads (e.g., extremely bursty or heavy-tailed API latency distributions beyond what was tested).

strengths: Clear and well-supported motivation: Section 3 provides concrete empirical evidence (queueing latency CDFs, goodput vs. request rate, batch-token sweep, API-return-length analysis) that FCFS scheduling and static batch-token limits are responsible for poor effective throughput in augmented LLM serving, giving the reader confidence that the identified problems are real and significant for this workload.

The two-stage scheduling design is a sensible and reasonably novel extension of InferCept's context-handling logic: Stage I uses predicted output length/API duration/return length to form an initial scheduling value, and Stage II corrects this value with observed runtime information, explicitly addressing prediction-error amplification that a naive single-stage SJF-like scheduler would suffer from.

Proposition 1 gives a clean theoretical justification for why total-length-based scheduling (used in prior general LLM serving work) is insufficient for augmented LLM requests and that API return length must be treated separately, strengthening the conceptual contribution.

Extensive empirical evaluation: multiple hardware platforms (4090, H800, 2xA100), two models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B), two realistic datasets (Merge, ToolBench), three workload types (Poisson, fixed-count, Gamma/bursty), and several metrics (goodput, TTFT, normalized latency, SLO attainment, P95 tail latency, TPOT), plus an ablation study isolating the dynamic batching and scheduling components and a breakdown showing negligible prediction overhead.

Reported gains (up to 33x goodput, up to ~96% TTFT reduction) are large and consistent across settings, and the ablation in Fig. 10/Table 4 supports the claim that both proposed components (dynamic batching and two-stage scheduling) contribute complementary improvements.
weaknesses: The paper only compares against vLLM and InferCept, both of which use FCFS scheduling; it does not compare against other length/SJF-prediction-based LLM schedulers mentioned in related work (e.g., learning-to-rank scheduling, S3, embedding-based scheduling, FastServe's preemptive time-slicing). Since the core claimed contribution is the scheduling algorithm, omitting scheduling-focused baselines makes it hard to isolate how much of the large improvement stems from the augmented-LLM-specific insights (API return length, context-handling awareness) versus simply moving away from FCFS to any length-aware or preemptive scheme (the paper's own 'random scheduling' experiment in §3.1 already shows large gains from simply breaking FCFS order).

The output-length predictor achieves only 65% accuracy on the Merge dataset (and MSE ~5s for API call time on one dataset), yet there is no sensitivity analysis showing how scheduling/throughput performance degrades as prediction accuracy worsens, nor an ablation comparing Stage I only vs. Stage I+II to quantify how much the runtime correction actually compensates for prediction error.

The scheduling value computation involves numerous hand-crafted cost formulas (Eqs. 4-26) with several hyperparameters (anti-starvation coefficient α, batching bounds β_low/β_high, γ for paused-memory preemption, offline-profiled target_max). No sensitivity study is provided for these hyperparameters, and it is unclear how they are tuned or how robust the system is to misconfiguration or to different hardware/model combinations without re-profiling.

The per-iteration computational overhead of computing/sorting scheduling values for all queued requests (with multiple cost terms per policy per request) is not analyzed for scalability as queue size or request rate grows; only the end-to-end time breakdown (<1% for 'Predict') is shown, which does not capture the cost of the scheduling-value computation and sorting itself.

No code, artifact, or detailed hyperparameter settings are provided for reproducibility, and some experimental details (e.g., exact SLO thresholds in different figures/tables, which appear to vary, and how the predictor's bucketed-classification outputs map to continuous cost formulas) are not fully specified.

The memory/cost model assumes a simple per-token KV footprint M and homogeneous forward-pass time T^fwd, which may not generalize well to modern attention variants (GQA/MQA, varying KV cache compression) or to multi-GPU/tensor-parallel settings beyond the two configurations tested, raising questions about broader applicability.

Presentation is heavily equation-driven (over 20 numbered equations across Sections 3-4) without much high-level intuition or pseudocode walkthrough in the main text (pseudocode is relegated to the appendix), which may hurt accessibility for readers trying to quickly grasp the scheduling logic.

strengths: Strong empirical motivation: Section 3 provides clear, quantitative evidence (Figures 2-4, Table 1) that FCFS/SJF scheduling and fixed token budgets are suboptimal for augmented LLM serving, effectively justifying the paper's design choices before presenting the method.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: experiments span four model/GPU configurations (GPT-J-6B/RTX4090, OPT-13B/H800, Vicuna-13B/2xA100, Llama-3-70B/4xA100), two datasets (INFERCEPT, ToolBench), and two workload types (Poisson, Gamma with varying burstiness), consistently showing large and consistent gains over vLLM, INFERCEPT, and SSJF baselines.

Thorough ablations and robustness analyses: the paper includes component-wise ablation (Table 2), sensitivity to hyperparameter β (Table 5, Appendix D.3), robustness to prediction error injection up to 50% (Figure 8), robustness to bursty arrivals (Table 7), scheduling overhead scaling with paused requests (Table 6), memory occupancy analysis (Figure 18), and comparison against a recent memory-based SJF baseline (MARS/Shahout et al., Appendix D.6), which collectively strengthen confidence in the claims.

Clear problem formalization: the request lifecycle modeling (Eq. 1, Figure 5) and space-time cost model (Eq. 5) provide a principled and interpretable way to capture heterogeneous, multi-stage resource consumption induced by external calls, which is a genuine conceptual contribution beyond simply combining known techniques.

Latency breakdown (Figure 9) and SLO attainment analysis (Appendix D.8) help attribute the goodput improvements specifically to reduced queuing delay, strengthening the causal story behind the reported gains.
weaknesses: The theoretical approximation guarantee (Appendix E) applies only to a simplified, static, single-iteration 0-1 knapsack abstraction with fixed values/costs, and the authors themselves acknowledge it does not extend to the actual online, multi-stage, feedback-driven scheduling problem; its inclusion therefore adds limited rigor to the paper's core claims.

Reproducibility is not clearly addressed: there is no mention of code or artifact release, and several implementation details (e.g., exact BERT predictor training data/features, hardware-specific tuning of β_low/β_high, Tmax) are not fully specified, making independent replication difficult.

The output-length predictor achieves only 65% bucket accuracy on the INFERCEPT dataset (vs. 85% on ToolBench); while the paper argues robustness via feedback refinement (Section 6.3), this robustness is only validated with synthetic, symmetric noise injection rather than the actual (likely biased) prediction errors from the trained BERT model itself.

The ablation study (Table 2) is conducted under a single configuration (OPT-13B, H800, 3.0 req/s, INFERCEPT dataset), leaving open the question of whether the relative contributions of the two components (token budget vs. scheduling) generalize across other models/datasets/load levels.

The scheduling value formula V_i = 1 + β·w_i (Eq. 2) is a simple heuristic without deeper theoretical justification; while β sensitivity is empirically explored, there is no analysis of why this particular linear form is appropriate or optimal relative to alternative formulations.

The comparison with MARS relies on the authors' own re-implementation since the original prediction model is unavailable for the INFERCEPT workload, which, despite stated efforts at fairness, introduces potential risk of implementation bias favoring AugServe.

The core technical contribution is an evolutionary extension of INFERCEPT (adding state-aware scheduling and dynamic token budgeting on top of existing context-handling policies) rather than a fundamentally new paradigm, somewhat limiting originality, though the execution and empirical validation are strong.

strengths: Addresses a practical and increasingly important problem: efficient serving of augmented/tool-calling LLMs under SLO constraints, with clear motivating examples (Figures 2-4, Table 1) that ground the two identified challenges (HoL blocking from FCFS scheduling, and static batch-level token budgets).
The request lifecycle formalization (service segments, context-handling-policy-dependent cost) gives a reasonably clean abstraction for reasoning about scheduling in the presence of external calls.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B, Vicuna-13B, Llama-3-70B), multiple GPU platforms, two datasets, and two workload types, plus thorough appendix material (ablations, β-sensitivity, prediction-error injection, bursty arrivals, tail latency, SLO attainment, memory occupancy, scheduling overhead).
Ablation study (Table 2) and latency breakdown (Figure 9) help isolate the separate contributions of the dynamic token budget and the state-aware scheduler, showing both are needed.
Robustness analysis to prediction noise (Figure 8) is a useful sanity check given the system relies on a learned predictor.
weaknesses: Soundness gap between the stated scheduling objective and the evaluation metric: the knapsack formulation (Eq. 2-3) optimizes an ad hoc linear combination of throughput and elapsed waiting time, with no explicit encoding of the TTFT/normalized-latency SLO thresholds used in evaluation; it is not clearly justified why maximizing this value density should translate into higher goodput under hard SLO deadlines, beyond empirical demonstration.

The theoretical contribution (Appendix E) is a standard 1/2-approximation for a static 0-1 knapsack with fixed, known values/costs—this does not match the actual online, multi-stage, feedback-driven problem AugServe solves, and the authors themselves concede it does not extend to the real setting, making its inclusion of limited value for supporting the paper's central claims.

Core techniques are largely combinations of existing ideas: value-density greedy knapsack scheduling (classic), the context-handling waste formulas are directly reused from INFERCEPT (Eq. 12-15), and the dynamic token budget is a natural extension of free-memory-based budgeting (Zheng et al., 2025) to include reclaimable memory. The novelty is more incremental/integrative than conceptually new.

The reported improvements are extremely large (6.5-7.5× goodput over vLLM, 4.7-5.7× over INFERCEPT), which raises fairness concerns: it is unclear whether baselines (vLLM, INFERCEPT) were run with well-tuned fixed token budgets or left at defaults, especially given the paper's own finding (Table 1) that optimal budget is highly workload/hardware dependent. Without clarifying baseline tuning, part of the claimed gain may stem from an uneven comparison rather than the proposed scheduling algorithm per se.

Prediction module accuracy is modest on the INFERCEPT dataset (65% bucket accuracy for output length), and while a robustness study is provided, it only injects synthetic multiplicative noise rather than evaluating with the actual (imperfect) learned predictor end-to-end in the main results, leaving open how much the reported main results already benefit from idealized/overfit predictions.

No mention of code or artifact release, and several system-specific hyperparameters (β, βlow, βhigh, bucket discretization, aging policy) are introduced without a principled or automated tuning procedure, which may hinder reproducibility and generalization to new models/workloads beyond those tested.

The MARS (Shahout et al., 2025b) baseline was reimplemented by the authors rather than using an official implementation, and other closely related embedding/memory-based schedulers (e.g., Shahout et al., 2025a) are not compared, limiting confidence that AugServe's advantage holds against the strongest alternative systems.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any limitations or broader considerations of deploying such scheduling systems (e.g., fairness across tenants, potential starvation under the greedy/value-density policy for long-waiting large requests).

strengths: Clear and well-supported motivation: the paper presents concrete empirical evidence (Figs. 2-4, Table 1) showing that FCFS/SJF scheduling and static token budgets fail under external-call-augmented workloads, grounding the two identified challenges (HoL blocking and fixed token budgets) in measured system behavior rather than assumption.

The proposed request lifecycle model (segments with prefill/decode/wait/resumption stages) is a natural and useful abstraction that cleanly captures the multi-round, state-dependent nature of augmented LLM inference, and the space-time cost formulation provides a principled way to unify heterogeneous resource costs across stages and context-handling policies.

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation: experiments span four models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B, Vicuna-13B, Llama-3-70B), multiple GPU configurations (RTX4090, H800, multi-A100), two datasets, two workload types (Poisson, Gamma with varying burstiness), and numerous ablations (component-wise ablation, β sensitivity, prediction-error robustness, scheduling overhead vs. paused-request count, memory occupancy, tail latency, SLO attainment, comparison to an additional re-implemented baseline MARS). This breadth substantially strengthens the credibility of the claimed gains.

The system demonstrates large, consistent improvements (geometric mean 6.5x/4.7x over vLLM/INFERCEPT, and further gains over SSJF and MARS) across nearly all tested configurations, and the ablation (Table 2) convincingly shows both proposed components (dynamic token budget and state-aware scheduling) contribute complementary gains.

The paper includes a lightweight prediction module with reported overhead (<0.1% of latency) and explicitly tests robustness to prediction noise (Fig. 8), addressing a natural concern about reliance on learned predictors.

A theoretical approximation analysis (Appendix E) is provided for the greedy value-density scheduling policy, and the authors are appropriately honest that this guarantee applies only to a simplified static subproblem, not the full online multi-stage system — a transparent and reasonably scoped theoretical contribution.
weaknesses: The approximation guarantee in Appendix E is for a static, single-iteration 0-1 knapsack relaxation with fixed values and costs; this bears limited relationship to the actual online, multi-stage, feedback-driven scheduling problem the paper addresses, and its practical significance for understanding AugServe's real-world behavior is modest despite being flagged as a discussion point.

Hyperparameter sensitivity (β, and token-budget clipping parameters βlow/βhigh/Tmax) is only evaluated in one hardware/model/dataset setting (OPT-13B on H800 with INFERCEPT); it remains unclear how robust the default values are across the other three model/GPU configurations used in the main results, raising concerns about tuning generalization.

The output-length predictor achieves only 65% bucket accuracy on the INFERCEPT dataset (vs. 85% on ToolBench), yet the paper does not analyze how this weaker prediction accuracy affects scheduling quality on that specific dataset beyond the injected synthetic-noise robustness test, which may not reflect realistic structured misprediction patterns (e.g., systematic underestimation for certain request types).

The main comparison baselines (vLLM, INFERCEPT, SSJF) are relatively dated or simple; the more directly relevant competitor MARS (memory-based SJF for augmented LLMs) is relegated to the appendix and is a self-reimplementation (since no official predictor for INFERCEPT is available), which could introduce implementation bias favoring AugServe. Comparison against other recent general-purpose schedulers (e.g., learning-to-rank scheduling, Sarathi-Serve-style chunked prefill) is absent.

All evaluations appear to rely on simulated/replayed external call durations and context lengths from the INFERCEPT/ToolBench datasets rather than live API calls with real network variability, which may understate real-world noise and jitter in external call behavior.

The paper does not report variance across repeated runs/seeds for its throughput, latency, or goodput measurements, making it difficult to assess the statistical reliability of the reported improvements, especially given some very large relative gains (e.g., near-zero baseline goodput at high load).

The dense mathematical notation (Table 4, multi-stage segment definitions, cost equations) could be streamlined; the core intuition (prioritize requests by value-per-resource, informed by predicted and then realized external-call costs) is somewhat obscured by heavy formalism relative to its conceptual simplicity.
